_meta: A randomized trial's outcomes broken down by arm (treatment vs control) and by adherence (patients who took what they were assigned vs those who did not), used to show why the effect must be estimated by intention-to-treat -- comparing the arms as randomized -- rather than by comparing adherers to non-adherers, because adherence is self-selected and predicts the outcome on its own (the healthy-adherer effect), so an adherence-based comparison confounds the treatment with health. Adherence is not assigned at random; healthier, more organized, more health-conscious patients are the ones who reliably take their medication, and those same traits improve outcomes independently of any drug. The famous demonstration is the placebo arm: patients given a sugar pill who adhered to it still did markedly better than those who did not, though the pill did nothing -- proof that adherence is a marker of health, not evidence of a treatment effect. So comparing patients who took the drug to those who did not (per-protocol or as-treated analysis) mixes the drug's effect with the health advantage of the adhering type, and inflates the estimate. Intention-to-treat compares the full arms by their random assignment, ignoring who actually adhered; randomization balanced the health types across arms, so the comparison is unconfounded, at the cost of estimating real-world effectiveness (which includes non-adherence) rather than the effect on perfect-takers. The fixture gives each arm x adherence cell its mean outcome and group size. These are the fixture; the within-arm adherer gaps (including the drug-free placebo gap that proves the bias), the naive per-protocol inflation, and the intention-to-treat arm comparison are computed.
